explanation: Exciter corresponds to earthquake source: In magnetic resonance imaging, the exciter generates a magnetic field that resonates atomic nuclei. In seismic imaging, the earthquake source generates seismic waves that cause underground rock formations to vibrate. Both are sources of signals.

Magnetic field corresponds to seismic wave: In magnetic resonance imaging, the magnetic field is the signal carrier generated by the exciter. In seismic imaging, seismic waves are the signal carriers generated by the earthquake source. Both are mediums that transmit information.

Magnetic corresponds to transmission speed: In magnetic resonance imaging, magnetism determines the characteristics of nuclear magnetic resonance. In seismic imaging, transmission speed determines the propagation characteristics of seismic waves in underground rock formations. Both are key factors that affect the transmission of signals.

background.source: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses strong magnetic fields, magnetic field gradients, and radio waves to generate detailed images of the anatomy and physiological processes of the body. Unlike other imaging techniques such as CT or PET scans, MRI does not involve the use of X-rays or ionizing radiation. By exciting the spin energy transition of hydrogen atoms using radio waves, and localizing it using magnetic field gradients, MRI generates images of the tissues and organs of the body, particularly water and fat, providing superior contrast in soft tissues, such as the brain and abdomen. MRI is widely used in hospitals and clinics for medical diagnosis, staging, and follow-up of various diseases. However, some patients may find the experience uncomfortable due to the length of the measurement and the loud noise of the machine. Magnetic implants and other non-removable metal in the body can also pose a risk to some patients, and in certain cases, exclude them from undergoing an MRI examination safely. MRI has proven to be a versatile imaging technique that has extended its utility beyond diagnostic medicine and biomedical research to capture neuronal tracts and blood flow in the nervous system.
background.target: Seismic imaging is a type of geophysical imaging technique that uses seismic waves to create an image of the subsurface of the earth. By analyzing the transmission speed of seismic waves through different materials, scientists can create a 2D or 3D model of the geological features beneath the surface. Seismic imaging is widely used in earthquake source analysis and also in various fields such as oil exploration, structural engineering, and environmental monitoring. It is a non-invasive way to study and understand the physical properties of the earth's subsurface. By using seismic tomography and reflection seismology, scientists can gain insights into the structural characteristics of geological formations and monitor changes over time.
